title: The sacred vessel
hook: the world is a sacred vessel; try to seize it and you ruin it (Tao Te Ching 29)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty-eight, and your line was be the valley. Where did you choose the soft way, and what flowed toward you? Day one thousand ninety-one.

A little kid with a bubble wand on a summer porch. One long breath, and out floats a bubble the size of a melon, wobbling, shining, turning colors. The kid is thrilled. And then does the obvious thing: reaches out with both hands to catch it. Pop. A wet spot on the palms, and a stunned face. Try again. Pop. The only way to keep watching the bubble is to leave it alone. Chapter twenty-nine of the Tao Te Ching says the whole world is like that bubble, and it says so to people who want to run things.
screen: `A BUBBLE ON A PORCH.` → `TWO HANDS REACH.` → `POP.`

segments.voice: First, trying to take the world. The chapter starts with someone who wants to take hold of the world and do something with it, fix it, run it, improve it. The speaker says plainly: I see that it can't be done. Second, a sacred vessel. Then the reason. The world, the chapter says, is a sacred vessel, a spirit-like thing. It can't be acted upon that way. In Legge's translation: "He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it." Grab it and you break it. Clutch it and it slips away. A vessel is a container, a made thing. Call it sacred, and it becomes something you handle carefully, with both hands, never roughly. Third, some lead, some follow. Next comes a list of how things actually are. Some go ahead, and some follow behind. Some breathe out warm, and some breathe out cold. Some are strong, some are weak. Some are up, some are down. The world has its own rhythms, its own back and forth, and a grabbing hand can't flatten them into one straight line. Fourth, no excess, no extremes. So what does the sage do? The chapter's answer is short: the sage lets go of the extreme, the extravagant, and the excessive. Not nothing. Not passivity. Just no overreach. Like the kid on the porch, learning, bubble after bubble, that the best way to keep the shining thing is to stand back and breathe.
screen: `TRYING TO TAKE THE WORLD.` · `A SACRED VESSEL.` · `SOME LEAD, SOME FOLLOW.` · `NO EXCESS, NO EXTREMES.` · then, large: `HOLD IT IN YOUR GRASP, AND LOSE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop forcing one outcome. Settle, and open your hands on your lap, palms up. Bring to mind one thing you're trying hard to make happen: someone's decision, a result at work, how a conversation is supposed to go. Feel where your mind is gripping it. Now, without giving up on it, loosen the grip a little, the way your hands are open now. Let it float in front of you like that bubble, still wanted, no longer squeezed. Keep the hands open. The bell holds the time.
The sacred vessel. Chapter twenty-nine's name for the world: a spirit-like thing that breaks when grabbed and slips away when clutched. Today's word.
Your line: don't grab it. When you feel your hands, or your mind, reaching to force something today, open them, and let it float a while longer. Day one thousand ninety-one.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty-nine as a caution against overreach: they work toward what they want while letting go of control over how it turns out.

myth: chapter twenty-nine says a strong enough ruler can take the world and improve it
the speaker says it can't be done: the world is a sacred vessel, and grabbing it destroys it.
the chapter lists how things differ: some lead, some follow, some strong, some weak
the world has its own back and forth, which a grabbing hand can't flatten.
the chapter tells the sage to do nothing at all
it says the sage lets go of the extreme, the extravagant and the excessive: no overreach, not no action.

fork.setup: you've been handed the chance to take hold of the world and fix it your way. chapter twenty-nine is open in front of you. what does it say?
options: grab it firmly, and set it straight.
it can't be done: grab it and you destroy it.
take half, and leave the rest.
fork.reveal: "he who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it." the world is a sacred vessel.

original.note: Chinese, tiānxià shénqì: all under heaven is a sacred vessel, from Tao Te Ching 29.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sacred vessel is a holy cup in a temple.
what it means: the world itself, which breaks when grabbed and slips away when clutched.
what a scholar hears: tianxia shenqi, all under heaven a spirit-vessel, and a sage who lets go of the extreme, the extravagant and the excessive.

sources.quoted: He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching, chapter 29 (taking the world; the spirit-vessel; leading and following; letting go of excess)

notes: Verify the Legge 1891 wording: 'He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it.'

The rest of chapter 29 is paraphrased. Legge renders 天下 as 'the kingdom' and 神器 as 'a spirit-like thing'; the teach uses 'the world' and 'a sacred vessel' (per the outline) and mentions 'spirit-like'. Confirm.
The teach glosses 器 only as a container, a made thing; no further lexical claim. Confirm.
The list of contrasts (lead/follow, warm/cold breath, strong/weak, up/down) varies between editions; confirm against the received text.
去甚，去奢，去泰 rendered as 'the extreme, the extravagant, and the excessive'. Confirm.
The bubble scene is an illustration, not a source.
